strengths: Novel and well-motivated application of test-time training (TTT) as a streaming long-term memory mechanism for video LLMs, extending prior TTT formulations with a long-span prediction objective that is shown via ablation (Fig. 8, Table 10) to specifically help retention at larger temporal distances between query and evidence.

The proposed ELViM benchmark addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in evaluating episodic/procedural memory in streaming video LLMs (learning from content observed tens of minutes to hours earlier), with a reasonably careful filtering pipeline designed to rule out shortcut answering (Table 6 shows near-chance accuracy without full video and near-ceiling with full video, supporting question validity).

Extensive and informative ablations: comparison of token compression strategies (merging/clustering/discarding), TTTMEM vs Mamba-2 vs vanilla TTT-video, two-stage training contribution, memory-size scaling (Fig. 6), frame-count scaling (Fig. 7), prediction span sweep (Table 10), and deepstack embedding design choice (Table 8) all lend credibility to individual design decisions.

All baselines are reimplemented on the same backbone (Qwen3-VL 8B) and same training data, which is a fair and controlled comparison methodology that isolates the contribution of the memory mechanism itself rather than confounding with backbone/data differences.

Consistent, sizeable improvements are reported across multiple benchmarks (Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, ELViM, StreamingBench), and efficiency numbers (Table 3, Appendix D) suggest the added TTTMEM/reading overhead is modest relative to baseline streaming methods, supporting practical deployability claims.
Useful qualitative case studies (Appendix C) illustrating concrete failure modes of non-streaming and PEMF baselines versus the proposed model, adding interpretive value beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: ELViM's question generation, distractor creation, and initial filtering are performed almost entirely by Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL, with only a final 'human collation' step described in one sentence; there is no inter-annotator agreement, no description of annotator qualification, and no analysis of how many questions were rejected/modified during human review, raising concerns about annotation quality and potential model-generation artifacts/biases.

The core technical contribution (TTTMEM) is an incremental extension of existing TTT formulations (Sun et al. 2024; Dalal et al. 2025), primarily adding an auxiliary long-span reconstruction loss; while empirically useful (~1-2% gains in Table 2), the conceptual novelty is limited and the mechanism is not analyzed beyond accuracy deltas (e.g., no analysis of what information the fast weights actually retain).

All experiments use a single backbone (Qwen3-VL 8B); no results are shown with a different LLM backbone or visual encoder to establish that the TTTMEM/reading gains generalize beyond this specific architecture.

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 1-2% differences in some ablation rows) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The claimed '3-hour' streaming capability is demonstrated concretely only via LVBench-style long videos; ELViM's merged videos cap at 90 minutes and average ~49 minutes (Table 4), so the flagship long-duration claim is not directly stress-tested by the newly introduced benchmark.

The modality-aware memory reading mechanism (Section 3.3) is described in dense notation without much intuitive explanation or a simplified pseudo-code walkthrough, hurting reproducibility/accessibility for readers wanting to reimplement it precisely.

Dataset composition for ELViM is restricted to tutorial/how-to YouTube videos in 15 lifestyle categories, which may limit generalizability of memory evaluation to other domains (e.g., narrative video, surveillance, multi-agent interaction) relevant to future agent applications discussed in the introduction/impact statement.
